title: Currency arbitrage as a negative cycle
objectives: Detect a currency arbitrage with logarithms and Bellman-Ford.
Turn a product of rates into a sum with $-\ln(\text{rate})$ weights
Implement Bellman-Ford with negative-cycle detection and a tolerance

screens.title: Money from nothing
screens.prose: Each arrow is a quote: one unit of the first currency buys this many units of the second. You start and finish in the same currency. A loop that hands back more than you put in is an **arbitrage**.

state.caption: 1 GBP buys 1.27 USD, and so on

screens.question: Tap the three currencies of the loop that makes money.

hints.text: Follow the arrows round each loop and multiply the rates.
Start with 1 GBP and go to USD.
GBP to USD to EUR to GBP: $1.27 \times 0.92 \times 0.86 = 1.004824$. The other loops give less than 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the rates round each loop and look for a product above 1.

byKey.chf: That loop gives $1.142 \times 0.92 \times 0.95 = 0.998108$, a loss. Try the loop through GBP.

explain.text: Round GBP, USD, EUR the rates multiply to $1.27 \times 0.92 \times 0.86 = 1.004824$. So £1,000,000 comes back as £1,004,824 before costs. The loop through CHF returns only 0.998108 per unit.

screens.title: Where it breaks even
screens.prose: Keep GBP to USD at 1.27 and USD to EUR at 0.92. Move the EUR to GBP rate and watch what £1 becomes after one loop.
screens.question: Which EUR to GBP rate makes the loop exactly break even? Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: Break even means £1 comes back as exactly £1.
Solve $1.27 \times 0.92 \times r = 1$: $r = 1 / 1.1684 \approx 0.8559$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find $r$ with $1.27 \times 0.92 \times r = 1$.

byKey.now: At 0.86 the loop still makes 0.48%. Lower $r$ until the caption reads £1.000000.

explain.text: The loop pays $1.1684\,r$, so it breaks even at $r = 1/1.1684 = 0.855871$. A loop worth exactly 1 is not an arbitrage. That edge case will matter when we code it.

screens.title: Products into sums
screens.prose: Shortest-path algorithms add costs; arbitrage multiplies rates. Logarithms turn products into sums, as in Exponentials and Logarithms. Give each arrow the weight $w = -\ln(\text{rate})$. The GBP loop multiplies to 1.004824.
screens.question: What is the total weight round the GBP, USD, EUR loop? Give 6 decimal places.

hints.text: Work out $-\ln$ of each rate, then add the three.
This arrow's weight is $-\ln 1.27 = -0.239017$.

feedback.correct: The profitable loop has negative total weight.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add $-\ln(\text{rate})$ over the three arrows.

byKey.sign: You added $\ln(\text{rate})$. The weight is $-\ln(\text{rate})$, so the sign flips.
byKey.sum: You added the rates themselves. Converting money multiplies rates; only their logs add.
byKey.prod: That is the product of the rates. The weights are $-\ln$ of each rate, added.

explain.text: The weights add to $-\ln(1.004824) = -0.004812$. A product above 1 became a sum below 0: a **negative cycle**. So arbitrage detection is negative-cycle detection, which Dijkstra cannot do.

screens.title: Pass after pass
screens.prose: **Bellman-Ford** works with negative weights. It relaxes every edge, in a fixed order, and repeats. Here the edges are listed in the order C→D, B→C, A→B. Costs start at 0 for A and ∞ elsewhere.

state.caption: Relaxed in the order C→D, B→C, A→B

screens.question: Fill in the costs after each full pass. Write ∞ (or inf) where a cost is still unknown.

hints.text: In pass 1, C→D comes first, while C is still ∞.
Only A→B can do anything in pass 1.
Pass 1 sets B = 2. Pass 2 sets C = 5. Pass 3 sets D = 6.

feedback.correct: Each pass pushed the known costs one edge further.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Relax the edges in the listed order, one pass at a time.

explain.text: In the worst order, each pass extends the correct costs by one edge. A shortest route uses at most $V - 1$ edges, so $V - 1$ passes always suffice. Here $V = 4$ and we needed all 3.

screens.title: Write it
screens.prose: Write Bellman-Ford. Relax every edge $n - 1$ times. Then run **one more pass**: if any edge still improves a cost, a negative cycle can lower it for ever, so return `None`.
screens.question: Write `bellman_ford(edges, n, s)`: the list of cheapest costs from `s`, or `None` if a negative cycle is reachable.

widget.how: Check runs 9 hidden tests. Nodes are `0` to `n − 1` and `edges` holds `(u, v, w)` triples. Return the list of costs, with `math.inf` for unreachable nodes, or `None` if a negative cycle is reachable from `s`.

hints.text: Start with `[math.inf] * n` and set `dist[s] = 0`.
This chain is listed backwards, so it needs every one of the $n - 1$ passes.
Loop `for _ in range(n - 1)` over every `(u, v, w)`, setting `dist[v] = dist[u] + w` when smaller. Then one more loop: any improvement means return `None`.

feedback.correct: Your Bellman-Ford finds the costs and spots every reachable negative cycle.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 lists the chain backwards. `inf` for node 3 means you ran fewer than $n - 1$ passes.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 has the cycle 1, 2, 1 with total −2. Run one extra pass and return `None` if anything still improves.
byKey.test-6: Test 6 has a cycle of total exactly 0. That is not negative, so return the costs.

explain.text: The $n - 1$ passes cost $O(V \cdot E)$, slower than Dijkstra, but negative weights are allowed. The extra pass is the detector. An unreachable negative cycle stays at ∞, since $\infty + w$ is never smaller.

screens.title: Forgetting the log
screens.prose: A colleague skips the logarithm and weights each arrow with `w = -rate`, then runs Bellman-Ford on the hook's graph.
screens.question: Which loops does their code report as negative cycles?

options.text: Every loop, because every weight is negative
Only the GBP, USD, EUR loop
options.why: You applied the log in your head. With $w = -\text{rate}$, every arrow weighs less than 0, so every loop sums below 0.
Each weight is minus a positive rate, so every loop adds up to a negative number.

hints.text: What sign does $-\text{rate}$ have?
All rates are positive, so all weights are negative, and every loop is a negative cycle.

feedback.correct: Without the log, every loop looks like free money.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add up $-\text{rate}$ round any loop.

byKey.gbp: You expected only the profitable loop. With $w = -\text{rate}$, the losing CHF loop sums to −3.012, negative too.

explain.text: Adding rates measures nothing: money multiplies along a route. Only $-\ln(\text{rate})$ turns the product test, above 1, into a sum test, below 0. A rate of exactly 1 gets weight 0, as it should.

screens.title: Exactly one
screens.prose:
Two quotes with no spread: GBP to USD at 1.25 and USD to GBP at 0.8. The round trip is worth exactly $1.25 \times 0.8 = 1$, so no arbitrage.

```python
import math
w = -math.log(1.25) - math.log(0.8)
print(w < 0)
```
screens.question: What does it print?

options.why: In exact arithmetic the sum is 0. In floating point it comes out as $-5.6 \times 10^{-17}$, just below 0.
Both logs are defined, since both rates are positive. The code runs.

hints.text: Floating-point logs are rounded.
$\ln 1.25$ and $\ln 0.8$ are not stored exactly.
The sum comes out as $-5.55 \times 10^{-17}$, which is below 0, so it prints `True`.

feedback.correct: Rounding makes a break-even loop look like a tiny profit.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about rounding in floating point.

byKey.false: You trusted exact arithmetic. The computed sum is $-5.55 \times 10^{-17}$, so `w < 0` is `True`.

explain.text: A loop worth exactly 1 can come out a hair below zero. Real code counts an improvement only if it beats a tolerance, such as $10^{-9}$. No arbitrage worth trading is that small.

screens.title: Why the log works
screens.prose: We claimed a loop with rates $r_1, r_2, r_3$ makes money exactly when its weights $-\ln r_i$ sum below 0. Each line follows from the one before.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $r_1 r_2 r_3 > 1$, the loop makes money
$\ln r_1 + \ln r_2 + \ln r_3 > 0$, the log of a product is the sum of the logs
$(-\ln r_1) + (-\ln r_2) + (-\ln r_3) < 0$, multiplying by $-1$ flips the inequality

hints.text: Start from what an arbitrage means in money.
Take logs of both sides, split the log of the product, then multiply by $-1$.

feedback.correct: Profit above 1 is the same as weight below 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start with the product and change one thing per line.

byKey.d3: Splitting the log needs a log first: take $\ln$ of the product before you split it.
byKey.d4: The minus signs come last, once the logs are already summed.

explain.text: Each step is reversible, so the statements are equivalent. With our rates: $1.004824 > 1$, so $\ln 1.004824 = 0.004812 > 0$, and the weights sum to $-0.004812 < 0$.

screens.title: After costs
screens.prose: Real quotes are tighter. GBP/USD is 1.2700, EUR/USD 1.0850 and EUR/GBP 0.8543. The implied cross is $1.0850 / 1.2700 = 0.854331$, a hair above the quote. Going GBP to EUR to USD to GBP returns 1.0000359 per pound. Each conversion costs 1 bp in spread and fees.
screens.question: What is the profit or loss on £1,000,000 round the loop after costs, in pounds?

hints.text: Multiply the gross factor by $0.9999$ once for each of the three conversions.
The gross gain is about £36.

feedback.correct: A gross gain of £36 becomes a loss of about £264.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Apply the 1 bp cost three times, then subtract the £1,000,000.

byKey.gross: That is the gain before costs. Three conversions at 1 bp each cost about £300.

explain.text: The loop earns 0.36 bp gross and pays 3 bp in costs, so it loses about £264. Mispricings between liquid quotes are this small, so triangular arbitrage rarely survives costs. In the graph, the costs make each weight $-\ln(0.9999 \times \text{rate})$, and the cycle stops being negative.

screens.title: The detector
screens.prose: Now put it together. `rates[a][b]` is how many `b` one `a` buys. Map currencies to numbers, weight each quote $-\ln(\text{rate})$, and add a start node joined to every currency at weight 0, so every cycle is reachable. `bellman_ford(edges, n, s, eps)` is provided.
screens.question: Write `has_arbitrage(rates)`: `True` if some loop of conversions returns more than it starts with.

widget.solution:
import math


def has_arbitrage(rates):
    names = sorted(set(rates) | {b for a in rates for b in rates[a]})
    index = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(names)}
    n = len(names)
    edges = [(index[a], index[b], -math.log(r))
             for a in rates for b, r in rates[a].items()]
    edges += [(n, i, 0.0) for i in range(n)]   # a start joined to every currency
    return bellman_ford(edges, n + 1, n, eps=1e-9) is None
widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests. `bellman_ford(edges, n, s, eps=0.0)` is already defined; it ignores improvements smaller than `eps`. `RATES` is the hook's graph. Test 4 is a round trip worth exactly 1.

hints.text: Give each currency an index; the extra start node is index `n`.
The profitable loop here is GBP, USD, EUR.
Build `(index[a], index[b], -math.log(r))` for every quote, add `(n, i, 0.0)` for each `i`, and return `bellman_ford(edges, n + 1, n, eps=1e-9) is None`.

feedback.correct: Your detector finds the 1.004824 loop and ignores break-even and cost-eaten ones.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: Test 2 lowers EUR to GBP to 0.855, so no loop pays. `True` here means the weights are not $-\ln(\text{rate})$.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 is worth exactly 1. Rounding makes it look negative: pass `eps=1e-9`.
byKey.test-9: Test 9's profitable loop, JPY and KRW, cannot be reached from GBP. Add a start node joined to every currency.

explain.text: The start node reaches every currency at cost 0, so any negative cycle anywhere is reachable. The tolerance stops rounding noise from posing as profit. Run on £1,000,000, the hook's loop is worth £4,824 before costs.

ideas: A loop of conversions is an arbitrage when its rates multiply to more than 1.
With weights $-\ln(\text{rate})$, a product above 1 becomes a sum below 0: arbitrage is a negative cycle.
Bellman-Ford relaxes every edge $V - 1$ times; if one more pass still improves a cost, a negative cycle exists. Use a small tolerance.

formula.name: Arbitrage as a negative cycle
formula.note: Logs turn products into sums; the minus sign turns profit into negative cost.

summary.trap: Adding rates, or weighting by $-\text{rate}$, makes every loop look profitable; only $-\ln(\text{rate})$ is right.

quiz.prose: Bellman-Ford runs on a currency graph with 8 currencies and 40 quotes.
quiz.question: How many relaxations does it make in total, including the detection pass?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the passes, then multiply by the edges.

byKey.nodet: That is the $V - 1 = 7$ main passes. The detection pass adds 40 more.
byKey.v: That is 9 passes. There are $V - 1 = 7$ passes plus one to detect, 8 in all.

explain.text: Seven passes settle every cheapest cost, and one more detects a negative cycle. That is $8 \times 40 = 320$ relaxations: $O(V \cdot E)$.

quiz.prose: A dealer quotes GBP to USD at 1.2700 and USD to GBP at 0.7870.
quiz.question: Is the round trip GBP, USD, GBP an arbitrage?

options.why: You added the rates. Converting multiplies them: $1.27 \times 0.787 = 0.99949$.
One leg above 1 means nothing on its own. Only the product round the loop counts.

feedback.correct: The spread costs about 5 bp on the round trip.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the two rates.

explain.text: $1.27 \times 0.787 = 0.99949 < 1$: the bid-ask spread takes 5.1 bp. In weights, $-\ln 1.27 - \ln 0.787 = +0.000510 > 0$, not a negative cycle.

quiz.prose: A colleague suggests running Dijkstra on the $-\ln(\text{rate})$ weights instead of Bellman-Ford, since it is faster.
quiz.question: Why does that fail?

options.text: Any rate above 1 gives a negative weight, and Dijkstra needs every weight to be at least 0

options.why: Dijkstra works with any real weights that are not negative. The problem is the sign, not the type.

options.text: Dijkstra only works on undirected graphs
options.why: Dijkstra handles directed graphs; the l7 graphs were directed. The trouble is the negative weights.

feedback.correct: $-\ln 1.27 < 0$, so a popped node may not be final.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What sign does $-\ln(1.27)$ have?

explain.text: A rate above 1 has a positive log, so its weight $-\ln(\text{rate})$ is negative. Dijkstra's popped costs are then not final, and with a negative cycle there is no cheapest cost at all.
